Senses.Explanation: ‘Baizhang's wild fox’ names the public case in which a former abbot tells Baizhang Huaihai that his answer ‘does not fall under cause and effect’ left him in a wild-fox body for five hundred lives. When he repeats the question, Baizhang answers ‘not blind to cause and effect’; the elder says that he has shed the fox body and asks for an unnamed monastic's funeral. The records do not leave that contrast as a settled formula. Two unnamed monks dispute both halves: one says that not being blind still has not shed the fox body, while the other asks how not falling ever entailed one. Guishan Lingyou answers the raised story by shaking a door panel, and Wuzu Fayan tests Foyan Qingyuan with the named case. Later records make the title itself a reusable teaching object: Xiaoyin Daxin raises it in his chamber, Wansong Xingxiu comments under it as case eight, and Hongfu Ziwen, Shita Xuanmi Li, Yunju Shuai'an Fancong, and Chongjue Fakong turn it into verse or hall comment. The label therefore names this particular case and its later public testing, not a general fox symbol.

Senses.Explanation: Hundreds, thousands, myriads, and millions is an emphatic number governed by its counted noun. At an offering for the birthday of the venerable Huanyou, Yulin Tongxiu points to the portrait and says that the old man sitting there leaves everyone at a loss, habitually gains the advantage, and that anyone who passes through here is like a dragon finding water or a tiger leaning on a mountain, adding vigor where there is vigor and style where there is none. He then says that those called descendants of his teacher's lineage in the Ming realm number in the hundreds, thousands, myriads, and millions, before asking how many have attained great capacity. The expression is therefore an emphatic count governed by descendants.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make the top of a hundred-foot pole the place where gaining entry is still insufficient and a further step is demanded, questioned, or refused. Changsha Jingcen’s verse says that even one who has gained entry is not yet genuine and must step forward from the pole-top, with the ten directions as the whole body. Wumen transmits Shishuang’s question asking how to advance, and Fojian Huiqin comments on the moment of advancement. An unnamed monastic puts the fixed question to Fadeng, while Yanguan Qi’an counters by asking what use advancement would have. These divergent responses preserve the pole-top as a public challenge rather than a fixed ladder stage.

Senses.Explanation: Zhong Kui is the legendary demon-queller, attested 70 times in 43 texts. Chan records do not retell a complete outside biography; they put his name and familiar attributes to work in public answers, festival speech, verse, and appraisal. Asked for “the host within the guest,” Wuzu Fayan answers, “Zhong Kui's little sister” (鍾馗小妹). At the Double-Fifth festival, after a student says that a little ghost might display a trick, Wuzu Fayan replies, “Zhong Kui will frighten you” (鍾馗嚇你), then speaks of a protective talisman. Xiaoyin Xin makes the demon-queller dance eighteen beats (鍾馗解舞十八拍); Panshan Dabo Qian pictures him on a wall beside swords hanging in space (壁上畵鍾馗，空中懸劍戟); and Fushan Fayuan says at New Year that no strange thing is presently before them, so there is no need to paste up Zhong Kui (目前無異怪，不用貼鍾馗). His name can also be an unglossed answer: asked how to discuss words with no trace, Dongshan Shouchu says, “Zhong Kui does not read books” (鍾馗不讀書). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated use of the demon-catching figure, his household, dance, painted image, and protective posting as encounter answers and teaching-seat language; no further symbolic meaning is assigned.
